#9022. Playfool spotlights hidden digital labour in data centre cleaning game at the V&A

Photography and video by Nico Lejtreger

Visitors to the Victoria and Albert Museum in London vacuumed digital dust from an overheating data server in game installation The Server by art and design duo Playfool.

Handling a decommissioned data-centre vacuum formerly used in a data centre, players were tasked with vacuuming as much ‘dust’ as possible within 60 seconds from a replica data server.

The installation was designed to emulate the unseen physical labour tied to the technological infrastructure underpinning the AI boom, and to evoke the gamified optimisation strategies employed in Amazon fulfilment centres.

During their visit to one, the design duo “discovered the unique internal video games workers can play to gamify their tasks, displaying real-time performance rankings among peers”.

The Server game emerged as a means of surfacing the often overlooked physical labour that goes into maintaining the ever-expanding material infrastructure fuelled by the rapid growth of AI.

“We often overlook the fact that technologies are based on a material foundation, subject to the forces of an ever-changing environment, and thus requiring constant upkeep after being brought into existence”, Playfool’s Daniel Coppen and Saki Maruyama told Dezeen.

Their installation consists of a replica of technology brand Nvidia’s latest AI server and a vacuum module featuring a set of screens that visualise clouds of digital particulates and rank players’ performance metrics.

It was intended to show that our relationship to the digital world is less frictionless than we might think.

“Behind the frictionless, smooth interfaces on our screens is a messy entanglement with the material world”, the designers added.

Situated amid the priceless antiquities of the V&A, the installation draws a parallel between the hidden human labour that sustains the availability of both a museum’s collections and the digital infrastructure we are increasingly dependent upon.

In this way, the game “serves as a reminder that all creation comes with an infinite responsibility of maintenance”, the designers said.

“AI has been especially prone to this blind spot, due to both the black box nature of how it works and of the infrastructure behind it, from undersea fibre-optic cables to data centres”, Coppen and Maruyama explained.

With the US set to double its data centre building to keep pace with the boom in AI, and spending on data centre infrastructure projected to top $800 billion per year globally in 2026, the designers hope The Server will help interrogate the responsibilities of care generated by the contemporary AI boom.

Commissioned by the V&A Museum’s Emerging Designer scheme, Playfool intended for The Server installation to help create discussions around AI and digital caregiving such as cleaning and maintenance.

“We believe games are a powerful medium to provoke conversation about these complex topics, crystallising experiences and ideas through introducing new forms of agency”, Playfool said.

For more stories related to AI data centres, see this toy from Basrua that emits an “ear piercing hum” when squeezed, this 60-building data centre by Gensler and this East London data centre approved as part of Truman Brewery masterplan.

The Server exhibition took place from 12 to 18 September at The V&A. For more events in architecture and design, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

Photography and video by Nico Lejtreger

#9020. Sony revives classic Walkman headphones as MDR-3R

Japanese electronics company Sony has leaned into 1980s nostalgia with its remake of the original Walkman headphones, complete with colourful, interchangeable foam pads.

The MDR-3R, with its slim headband and sliding metal arms, looks almost exactly like the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979.

But the design now comes with a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices, feeding into the growing return to wired headphones.

The original MDR-3s pioneered the idea of modern portable headphones and have inspired a host of copycats – both then and now, as retro on-ear headphones have staged a comeback in recent years.

“The value of wired headphones is being rediscovered for their simplicity, ease of use, and freedom from charging or pairing,” Sony said.

The company went back to its archives and stuck close to the lightweight, open-ear design, adding interchangeable blue and orange foam pads and details in recycled plastic.

Sony even replicated the 1979 packaging and reengineered the headphones with the same 23-millimetre driver units to stay true to the original sound – although subtle refinements were apparently made to suit “modern listening preferences”.

On top of the USB-C connector, the product has been updated with a built-in microphone and an inline remote for controlling audio and calls.

Sony has also released a limited-edition version of the MDR-3R with red foam pads and a black headband in collaboration with Netflix‘s Stranger Things, celebrating their “shared 1980s inspiration”.

Retro gadgets have grown increasingly popular in recent years, as Gen Z has rediscovered gadgets such as cassette players, digicams and Tamagotchis.

The trend seems to have grown hand-in-hand with the rise of calm technology, as consumers have grown weary of modern tech.

#9019. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she says.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”

#9018. Does Magnesium Help You Lose Belly Fat?

We include products we think are useful for our readers. If you buy through links on this page, we may earn a small commission. Here’s our process

Magnesium is found in fatty fish, leafy greens, whole grains — and the supplement aisle.

The mighty mineral plays many essential roles in our bodies, but can it help tighten the belt buckle?

While magnesium can sneakily support weight loss in a few ways, that’s not its main gig.

“Magnesium alone is not a magic bullet for weight loss,” says Paunel Vukasinov, MD, a dual board-certified internist and obesity medicine specialist with Medical Offices of Manhattan.

“A comprehensive approach including diet, exercise, and other lifestyle changes are essential,” Vukasinov adds.

Here are a few ways magnesium may support weight loss, as explained by Vukasinov.

“Magnesium is not classified as an appetite suppressant,” Vukasinov says.

“However, by potentially stabilizing blood sugar and insulin levels, magnesium may reduce cravings and help prevent overeating. This effect can indirectly support weight loss.”

Vukasinov reminds us that no specific magnesium dosage is prescribed solely for fat loss.

With that in mind, the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for magnesium is:

Vukasinov says that sticking to the RDA ensures you meet your body’s needs without over-supplementing.

“Excessive intake does not enhance weight loss and may lead to adverse effects,” he adds.

According to Vukasinov, it’s best to get magnesium from food since a nutrient-dense diet, including whole foods, boosts your intake of other extra essentials like fiber, which improves overall health.

Here are some foods you can gobble up for the most magnesium:

If you know your diet isn’t cutting it, you can find magnesium supplements at major retailers, like Wal-Mart and Target, drug stores, or Amazon.

PSA: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not check the safety or effectiveness of dietary supplements, so it’s important to choose a reputable brand that undertakes third-party testing to prove the purity and quality of their products.

For some, magnesium supplements may cause a few unsavory side effects, including diarrhea, stomach upset, or cramping.

Remember that there are many forms of magnesium. Vukasinov points out that magnesium citrate or magnesium oxide can have a laxative effect (yikes).

Be sure you’re taking the best dose based on your RDA, and consider taking it with a meal to better avoid side effects.

Magnesium is not a miracle solution for weight loss, but getting enough of it can ensure that your body produces enough energy and gets enough sleep — both play a big hand in weight management.

Taking too much will have you gripping your belly with stomach pain or diarrhea, so stick to the daily recommended amounts.

#9016. Oshinówò Studio tops Lutyens-designed war memorial with glass prism to honour Sierra Leone's Carrier Corps

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated

The Commonwealth War Graves Commission has unveiled a memorial to the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Officially opened this weekend, the memorial designed by Oshinówò Studio sits on top of a war memorial designed by British architect Edwin Lutyens in 1931.

While the original memorial honoured soldiers who died in the first world war, it did not include the names of the 946 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps – men enlisted to transport supplies and materials – who also died in the war.

Oshinówò Studio extended the Lutyens-designed, stone memorial by adding a structural glass pyramid etched with the names of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps men.

“The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts,” said Oshinówò Studio founder Tosin Oshinówò.

“The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens’ existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. “

According to Oshinówò, placing the names of the carrier corps men higher than the soldiers was also a symbolic move.

“In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served,” she said.

“There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today.”

Along with the glass pyramid, the memorial also includes a laser beacon that will be illuminated on significant days of remembrance. According to the team, this column of light will be visible from up to five kilometres.

As part of the project, the 1930s memorial was also full restored by stonemasons and bronze specialists from the Commonwealth War Graves Commission.

Recent memorials featured on Dezeen include a “serene and contemplative” memorial to Queen Elizabeth II designed by Foster + Partners and a park in Ethiopia dedicated to the 157 victims of the Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 crash.

Photography by Tolu Sanusi / Oshinówò Studio unless stated

#9015. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

You’re just out of the shower and swiping on your favorite deodorant, expecting to stay fresh all day, but instead, your underarms decide to throw a tantrum. That’s a deodorant allergy in action!

While deodorants are supposed to be your BFF in the battle against body odor, they sometimes bring some unfriendly side effects, thanks to certain chemicals and fragrances that can turn your pits into an itchy nightmare.

#9012. EBBA Architects transforms former agricultural barn in Cornwall into a "calm sanctuary"

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.

Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.

EBBA Architects looked to restore the Dutch barn‘s original, open spatial character, expanding its area by almost a third with the addition of a pavilion-like extension that is framed by columns of white stone.

“The overall concept was about finding clarity in the form of the building and finding ways to add in a way that didn’t take away from the original character,” EBBA’s founding director, Benni Allan told Dezeen.

“Over the years the barn had gathered a series of piecemeal alterations that took away from the original simplicity. Our process involved removing later additions and then adding where felt most appropriate,” he added.

“The house is a place that will act as a place to enjoy the vast contrast of weather throughout the year, while also providing a calm sanctuary and background for family life.”

The ground-floor plan of Dutch Barn is based on the central position of an existing stair, around which a bathroom and storage core has been built to separate the more open kitchen and living spaces.

A row of full-height openings links the existing barn to its extension, where a long, uninterrupted space containing a skylit dining area and lounge opens out onto a covered colonnade via sliding doors.

“The intention is for the house to be used by the large family, and for there to be a blend between spaces,” Allan explained.

“We are always interested in making flexible arrangements in planform, to accommodate different ways of living.”

The home’s interior finishes were also guided by ideas of simplification, with plaster walls, concrete floors and gridded white-painted timber ceilings.

EBBA Architects wanted to emphasise material junctions, as seen in a new oak column in the kitchen, which has been rotated to highlight where it meets the flitch plates that connect it to the exposed ceiling beams.

Externally, this theme was extended into the design of the extension’s roof, which stops short of the edge of the stone columns to emphasise the point where the two meet.

The existing barn was clad in reused cedar shingles that were replaced where necessary, while the extension was built using white stone masonry that references the walls on the adjacent street.

“At first glance the house presents itself as a simple barn, but we like that a series of quite serious architectural moves have been complemented with some playful elements, such as the exaggeration of the junctions and the contrast between textured columns and clear, almost gallery-like floors,” explained Allan.

“We wanted the projecting roof and new columns to read as an independent object that reaches out into the garden and takes up the change in level, rather than as a continuation of the barn,” he added.

EBBA Architects has previously completed a cafe in Marylebone with clay plaster walls and an illuminated glass ceiling, and an apartment in London for its founder that is lined with Douglas fir.

Photography by Rikard Kahn and Benni Allan

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

Do this: Book at the 361-day mark with precision. QSuites availability is genuinely scarce. The readers who get this redemption are the ones who treat the booking window opening like a product launch. Set two calendar alarms — one for 362 days out as a reminder, one for 361 days out as a launch signal. Have your Privilege Club account open and your credit card details ready.

Do this: Confirm the aircraft before you transfer anything. Not every Qatar flight uses QSuites. Qatar operates multiple cabin configurations on its fleet, and even the same route can have different aircraft depending on the day. Always verify the aircraft type (Boeing 777-300ER or A350 with QSuites) in the booking flow before initiating a points transfer. Booking "Business Class" on a non-QSuites aircraft is a common and painful mistake.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou Points as your primary transfer partner. The instant transfer speed from Citi is a real operational advantage. When you find availability, you can transfer and book in a single session. With Capital One's 2–5 day transfer window, there's a risk the seat disappears before your Avios post. Prioritize earning Citi ThankYou Points if this redemption is a goal.

Do this: Add a Doha stopover. Qatar allows stopovers in Doha on award tickets. If your ultimate destination is beyond Doha — whether that's Asia, Africa, or the Indian subcontinent — building in a Doha layover costs nothing extra in points and gives you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, which is worth experiencing on its own terms.

Avoid this: Using Marriott Bonvoy as your primary transfer path. The 3:1 ratio means you need 225,000 Bonvoy points to get 75,000 Avios. Marriott points are valuable for hotel redemptions — burning them at a 3:1 ratio for airline miles is rarely optimal unless you have a massive surplus.

Avoid this: Waiting for a sale or hoping for better availability. Qatar doesn't run award sales. The award chart is fixed, and availability only decreases over time on popular routes. The readers who say "I'll book when something comes up" are the ones sharing their story about the year they almost flew QSuites.

Remember: Miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your Privilege Club account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every 36 months. A single small transaction resets the clock.

This redemption is purpose-built for the ChooseFI couple or family who has spent a year or two being intentional about travel rewards and is ready to cash in on the premium cabin experience they've been building toward. If you and a partner each hold a Citi Premier or Capital One Venture X and have been putting real spend on those cards, 150,000 combined points for two QSuites seats is a realistic 12–18 month accumulation target.

Minimum points required: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. For a couple, plan on 150,000 Avios. Have this balance confirmed before you begin the booking process.

This redemption earns a **Moderate** difficulty rating, and that's honest. The value is a 5/5 — there is almost no better use of transferable points in the entire loyalty ecosystem. But you'll earn that value. **What makes it hard:** First, **availability is legitimately limited.** QSuites seats don't sit open for weeks. Qatar releases a constrained number of award seats, and on popular routes, they go fast. This isn't a system you can approach casually. You need to search early and book decisively. Second, **the booking process has multiple steps.** Unlike a straightforward Chase Ultimate Rewards hotel redemption, this requires confirming availability on one platform, identifying points across potentially multiple credit card programs, executing a transfer, and booking on a separate airline's website. Each step has its own timing consideration. Third, **aircraft confirmation requires attention.** Not every Qatar flight is a QSuites flight, and the average traveler can easily book Business Class on a non-QSuites aircraft without realizing the difference. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Build your Citi ThankYou balance specifically for this redemption.** Instant transfers eliminate the timing risk that makes other transfer paths stressful. 2. **Set your 361-day calendar alert today**, even if your travel date is hypothetical. Practice the search so you know exactly what to look for. 3. **Use Qatar's own website for searching**, not third-party tools — Qatar award inventory is most accurately displayed on qatarairways.com. If you've successfully booked a domestic partner award before, you can absolutely do this. The moderate difficulty reflects the preparation required, not insurmountable complexity.

Log into your Qatar Privilege Club account and search for business class award space on your desired route. Look for flights showing QSuites availability — check the aircraft type (A350-1000 or 777-300ER with QSuites). This confirms what BA Avios can book since both programs are in oneworld.

Not all Qatar 777s have QSuites. Check SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to confirm the specific aircraft configuration. Routes to major US gateways (JFK, IAD, ORD, IAH, LAX, DFW) typically operate QSuites-equipped aircraft.

Once you confirm availability, transfer the required Avios from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming space.

Search for the same Qatar-operated flight on ba.com using your Avios. If the flight appears, book online. If you cannot find it online, call BA Executive Club to book partner award flights — agents can see availability that may not display on the website.

British Airways charges approximately 70,000 Avios one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights, plus taxes and fees typically between $30 and $80. Return flights are priced the same, making a round trip roughly 140,000 Avios total.

Yes, but finding 4 business class award seats on the same flight is challenging. Your best strategy is to search 330 days in advance when availability first opens, or check within 2-3 weeks of departure for last-minute releases. Consider splitting across two flights departing the same day if needed.

QSuites features a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a lie-flat bed, Bric's amenity kit with Diptyque products, and the option to create a Buddy Suite by lowering the partition between center seats. Standard Qatar business class uses a reverse herringbone or staggered layout without doors — still a solid product but a significant step below QSuites.

No. When you book Qatar Airways-operated flights using British Airways Avios, there are no fuel surcharges. You will pay the Avios cost plus minimal taxes and airport fees, typically $30 to $80 depending on the route. This is one of the key reasons the Avios route is preferred over booking through some other programs that impose carrier-imposed surcharges.

Qatar QSuites via British Airways Avios is the single best business class redemption available to ChooseFI community members. At roughly 70,000 transferable points for a $6,000 or more experience, the value per point is exceptional. The product itself — a fully enclosed suite with a door, lie-flat bed, and world-class service — redefines what business class can be. Whether you are heading to Doha, the Maldives, or Southeast Asia, routing through Qatar's hub gives you access to a global network at sweet spot pricing. Start searching 330 days out, have your transfer partners ready, and book the moment you find availability. This is the redemption that converts skeptics into travel rewards enthusiasts.

#9010. Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

The truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

In short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, says Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That said, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison says what’s most important is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

However, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research shows that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research shows chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

#9008. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#9007. Carsten Höller installs "largest" of his slides in Mexico City

Artist Carsten Höller has installed the largest-ever version of his architectural slides as part of a development in Mexico City led by local architecture studio Sordo Madaleno.

Mexico City Slides is Höller‘s latest slide installation yet and features four slides ranging from 12 to 38 meters in height and 31 to 90 meters in length.

The metallic slides with transparent sections cascade around the courtyard of the Antara development in Mexico City’s Polanco neighbourhood, a joint venture between architecture studio Sordo Madaleno and its development arm, SOMA.

It is part of the wider Colonia Granada district.

“Mexico City Slides, which is my largest project with slides so far, connects four different parts of the buildings that make up the new Antara destination,” said Höller.

Its courtyard location, curated by Arte Abierto, is between several buildings containing retail and offices, including an office for technology company Google. A 43-storey tower for a Mexico City Rosewood Hotel is also planned for the site.

The slides take people from various parts of the retail, hospitality and office programming down to a central outdoor landing area.

Höller emphasised the slides’ role in taking people out of their usual routine through a combination of “joy and fear”.

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants and from an art centre are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” said Höller.

“They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”

Höller continued, calling the slides “an existential experience of bare life, not unlike a ‘voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind'”.

The artist has designed multiple of these slides across the world. These include installations in a Florentine palazzo, woven through the Anish Kapoor-designed ArcelorMittal Orbit in London and, with a tower, at Vitra campus.

#9005. Dezeen Awards trophy updated using "one of humanity's oldest natural materials"

Photography courtesy of Corticeira Amorim

Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim has used sustainably harvested cork to refresh the latest edition of Dezeen’s iconic D-shaped trophy.

The trophies will be presented to this year’s winners at the Dezeen Awards party next week on 16 November at London’s Royal Opera House.

The event will bring together shortlisted studios, judges and the international architecture and design community to celebrate this year’s projects and reveal the 2026 winners, who will be the first to collect the new trophies.

Final tickets are available until 12pm London time on 11 November. Secure yours now.

An all-cork refresh for Dezeen Awards trophies

This year’s trophies have been produced in partnership with Corticeira Amorim, the world’s largest cork processing group, and mark the next material chapter for Dezeen’s trophy designs.

The updated design features an all-cork material palette that creates “a very direct encounter with the material”, according to Corticeira Amorim board member Cristina Amorim.

The group began by considering the trophy’s original design by Dutch studio Atelier NL, which was first created in 2018 and made from clay.

“The starting point was to preserve the recognisable form and graphic identity of the Dezeen Awards trophy, while allowing cork itself to become part of the design,” Amorim explained.

Cork is derived from the outer bark of the cork oak, which grows mainly in western Mediterranean countries such as Portugal, where Corticeira Amorim is based and has operated for over 150 years.

The material is renewable and recyclable. It is harvested without felling the tree, which naturally regenerates its bark to be harvested again at intervals of at least nine years.

Cork can also sequester carbon while replacing other, more polluting materials.

Beyond its sustainability credentials, the material is also remarkably light, resilient and adaptable in its nature.

“There is an interesting challenge in cork – it is one of humanity’s oldest natural materials, yet we are still discovering what it can do,” Amorim said.

This challenge spurred the development of different cork compositions, textures and finishes, after which a set of grains and colour references were selected to distinguish winner tiers while keeping a consistent visual language across the collection.

The winners of this year’s project categories, project of the year and Designers of the Year will each receive one of the bespoke cork trophies.

The project marks a continuation of Corticeira Amorim’s collaboration with architecture and design initiatives, revealing what Amorim sees as the “side of cork people may not expect”.

In 2024, the cork manufacturer produced the installations for City Cortex, a major arts programme that took place across the city of Lisbon.

The programme brought together internationally recognised architects and designers to create cork-based interventions for public and semi-public spaces, including Eduardo Souto de Moura, Diller Scofidio + Renfro and Yves Béhar.

Other notable projects also include Herzog & de Meuron and Ai Weiwei’s sunken 2012 Serpentine Pavilion, as well as product collaborations with designers including Jasper Morrison, the Bouroullecs and Naoto Fukasawa, showcasing the material’s broad potential.

“What makes cork surprising is its versatility: the same natural material can be transformed in so many different ways – some of them still unconceived,” Amorim said.

Reflecting on this year’s trophies, Amorim said: “cork is not simply associated with the awards – it becomes part of the award itself.”

“What we like about the final result is its simplicity,” she continued.

“The shape belongs unmistakably to the Dezeen Awards, but the texture, warmth, grain and natural variation belong unmistakably to cork.”

Previous editions of the Dezeen Awards trophy have explored materials including a compound of micro-paper, wood from London street trees and clay used to make the traditional yellow bricks found in the UK’s capital.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#9004. 7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

But this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

Besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that issue with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi says.

Nielsen also takes issue with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a big, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she says.

In other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi says. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi says—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.)

That said, this issue can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen says.

In Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she says. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related issues like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same issue, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.)

“In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen says. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

On the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen says—and “protein is a big bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

“Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.)

“Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi says. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

#9002. Gustaf Westman unveils full Disney collection featuring Donald Duck bookstand and Pluto mirror

Swedish designer Gustaf Westman‘s full collaboration with media company Disney, which saw him reimagine familiar Disney details “through his own design language”, has been revealed.

The collection, which launches on 15 November, features homeware, accessories and glassware, alongside made-to-order furniture.

Among the furniture pieces are a bookstand designed to resemble Donald Duck, a Goofy coffee table and Mickey dresser, as well as a Pluto mirror.

Each takes recognisable features from the Disney characters and turns them into parts of the design object, with the Donald bookstand decorated with his hat and duck feet.

Westman told Dezeen he wanted to work with Disney because he grew up with the brand.

“Disney is part of so many people’s childhood, including mine,” the designer explained.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” he continued.

His aim was to create something new while using details that are deeply familiar to many.

“I wanted to take those familiar details and reimagine them through my own design language, with sculptural, playful forms in bold proportions, and bring that sense of joy into people’s homes,” Westman said.

The collection also includes smaller objects such as a vase designed to look like Mickey’s trousers, a glass that evokes Minnie Mouse and a candelabra resembling Donald Duck.

There is also merch, including a T-shirt, hoodie, keychains, hairbands and pins.

Westman’s own favourite object is the Mickey Tumbler, which was one of the first objects from the collection to be revealed.

“The Mickey Tumbler is my favourite,” he said.

“It combines my chunky shapes with Mickey’s signature colours and an ear-shaped lid, so both worlds are instantly recognisable without overcomplicating the design.”

Disney and Westman are hosting a series of pop-up experiences in Tokyo, New York and Paris to launch the collection before it is released online.

Disney also targeted the homeware and interior industries in 2022, when it launched its own homeware brand.
